title: Why you cannot quietly change history
summary: Each commit's hash covers its tree and its parent, so every commit's identity depends on everything before it. Try to alter an old commit in place and watch the whole chain refuse.
mental_model: A commit's sha covers its tree, its parent's sha, the author and the message. Change anything anywhere and every descendant's sha changes too. History is not protected by permissions — it is protected by arithmetic.

write.content:
opening balance: 1000
payment out: 250
payment out: 100

opening balance: 1000
payment out: 250
payment out: 100
closing balance: 650

steps.title: See the chain
steps.why: Each commit records its parent's sha. `--format='%h parent=%p'` makes the links visible — this is the chain that makes tampering detectable.
steps.expect: Every commit naming its parent, back to the root.

steps.title: Try to change an old commit in place
steps.why: Build a new tree with an altered ledger and a new commit object with the SAME parent as the original. It succeeds — and produces a different sha, because the content differs. There is no way to make it produce the original sha.

actions.run: sh -c 'git commit-tree $(git write-tree) -p $(git rev-parse HEAD~3) -m "Record payment of 250" > .git/forged-sha'

steps.expect: Two different shas for two different contents — as designed.

verify.label: the altered commit gets a different sha, always

steps.title: Splice the forgery in and see what breaks
steps.why: Point a branch at the forged commit. It is a valid commit — but the two commits that came after the original still name the ORIGINAL sha as their parent, so they cannot be reached from here. The tamper cannot be hidden inside the existing chain.
steps.expect: Two separate histories — the forgery is a fork, not a substitution.

verify.label: the forged chain stops where the real one continues

steps.title: Confirm the descendants still point at the original
steps.why: Read the parent sha recorded in the commit after the tampered one. It names the original — and always will, because that sha is baked into its own hash.
steps.expect: The child names the original commit, not the forgery.

steps.title: The only way to change an old commit
steps.why: Rewrite everything after it too. That is exactly what rebase and filter-branch do — and every downstream sha changes, which is why anyone else's clone notices immediately.
steps.expect: Identical messages and identical trees — and every single sha in the chain is different, because the author field changed in the first commit and that ripples all the way up.

steps.title: Corrupt an object and let fsck catch it
steps.why: The filename of an object IS the hash of its content, so any change makes the two disagree. `fsck` recomputes and reports — which is why silent corruption, from disk or from malice, is not a thing git tolerates.

actions.run: sh -c 'sha=$(git rev-parse HEAD~2); f=.git/objects/${sha%${sha#??}}/${sha#??}; chmod u+w "$f" 2>/dev/null; printf "tampered" > "$f"; echo damaged'

steps.expect: An error naming the exact object whose content no longer matches its name.

verify.label: fsck detected content that does not match its hash

steps.title: What signing adds on top
steps.why: Hashing proves the history is internally consistent; it does not prove who wrote it — anyone can forge a chain from scratch. A GPG or SSH signature on the commit or tag is what binds it to a person, and `%G?` reports the verification status.
commands: sh -c 'git config --get user.signingkey || echo "no signing key configured"'
steps.expect: %G? shows N — no signature — for every commit here.

verify.label: altered content can never reproduce the original sha
a forged commit forks history rather than replacing it
verify.hint: descendants record their parent's sha in their own hash

verify.label: rewriting an old commit changed every sha after it
verify.hint: compare against the tip recorded before the rewrite — main's objects are deliberately damaged by the last step

verify.label: fsck detects an object whose content was altered

pitfalls: Hash chaining proves consistency, not authorship. Signing commits or tags is what proves who made them.
sha-1 is weakened against collision attacks; git uses a hardened variant that detects the known attack, and sha-256 repositories exist. For accidental corruption either is more than adequate.
Every rewrite tool changes downstream shas. If a tool claims to edit an old commit without changing later shas, it is lying or it is not git.
A tampered object in a packfile shows up as a pack error rather than a loose-object error, but fsck catches both.
cheatsheet: the raw commit, with its tree and parent
recompute every hash and report mismatches
sign, to bind history to a person
the only way to alter an old commit: rewrite everything after it
